notes.front: What are the Volunteer Standards of Conduct (VSC)?
notes.back: The standards of conduct, set out on Form 13615, developed specifically for running free tax preparation programmes.
notes.explanation: Form 13615 applies them to all conduct and ethical behaviour affecting the VITA/TCE programmes.
notes.example: Like a professional code of ethics, but written for volunteers at free tax sites rather than for paid preparers.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Volunteer Standards of Conduct (VSC)”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The Volunteer Standards of Conduct were developed specifically for the operation of free tax preparation programs. Form 13615, Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, applies to all conduct and ethical behavior affecting the VITA/TCE programs.

notes.front: How does SPEC define unethical?
notes.back: Not conforming to agreed standards of moral conduct, especially within a particular profession.
notes.explanation: In most cases, unethical behaviour is done with the intent to disregard established laws, procedures or set policies.
notes.example: Like a referee knowingly ignoring the rulebook, as opposed to one who simply misreads it.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Unethical Defined”, p. 2
notes.evidence: IRS-SPEC defines unethical as not conforming to agreed standards of moral conduct, especially within a particular profession. In most Confidentiality, and Civil Rights cases, unethical behavior is acted upon with the intent to disregard the – A Public Trust established laws, procedures, or set policies.

notes.front: May VITA/TCE sites and volunteers offer clients a refund anticipation loan (RAL)?
notes.back: No, not when preparing federal or state tax returns.
notes.explanation: SPEC still encourages partnering with banks or credit unions to help unbanked taxpayers open accounts.
notes.example: Like a “not offered here” sign at the preparation table: while a federal or state return is being prepared, a RAL is never on offer.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: SPEC encourages partnering with banks or credit unions to promote unbanked taxpayers to open bank accounts. However, sites and volunteers cannot offer clients refund anticipation loans (RAL) or refund anticipation checks (RAC) when preparing federal or state tax returns.

notes.front: Besides the refund anticipation loan, which refund product may VITA/TCE sites and volunteers not offer clients?
notes.back: The refund anticipation check (RAC).
notes.explanation: The ban covers both products whenever federal or state returns are being prepared.
notes.example: Like a second item on the same “not offered here” sign: named separately from the RAL, banned in the same sentence.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: However, sites and volunteers cannot offer clients refund anticipation loans (RAL) or refund anticipation checks (RAC) when preparing federal or state tax returns.

notes.front: Which body, together with SPEC, found unacceptable practices at a few VITA/TCE sites in past filing seasons?
notes.back: The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA).
notes.explanation: In response, SPEC enhanced the Volunteer Standards of Conduct.
notes.example: Like an independent auditor whose findings made the club tighten its rulebook.
introduces: Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Why do we have Ethics Training?”, p. 1
notes.evidence: During past filing seasons, the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) and IRS-SPEC discovered unacceptable practices at a few VITA/TCE sites. In response to these issues, IRS-SPEC enhanced the Volunteer Standards of Conduct.
uses: Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration

notes.front: What is the SPEC Volunteer Registry?
notes.back: A register to which volunteers and partners released for egregious actions and willful violations of the VSC can be added.
notes.explanation: The SPEC director decides whether a volunteer or partner is added.
notes.example: Like a sports body’s list of banned officials, but for VITA/TCE volunteers and partners.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Volunteer Registry”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Volunteers and partners released from the VITA/TCE program for egregious actions and willful violations of the Volunteer Standards of Conduct, can be added to the IRS-SPEC Volunteer Registry. The IRS-SPEC director will determine if a volunteer or partner should be added to the registry.

notes.front: What is the external referral process (VolTax)?
notes.back: The route by which taxpayers, volunteers, coordinators and others report potential unethical problems at VITA/TCE sites.
notes.explanation: Reports go by email to SPEC headquarters, copying the partner and the local SPEC territory office as appropriate.
notes.example: Like a whistle-blowing hotline, but it is an email address open to taxpayers as well as volunteers.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “External Referral Process”, p. 15
notes.evidence: If an unethical situation is discovered the external referral process (VolTax) provides taxpayers, volunteers, coordinators, and others an avenue to report potential unethical problems encountered at VITA/TCE sites. Volunteers and taxpayers can send an email to SPEC headquarters ts.voltax@irs.gov and copy the partner and the local SPEC territory office as appropriate.

notes.front: How is due diligence defined for VITA/TCE volunteers?
notes.back: The degree of care and caution reasonably expected from, and ordinarily exercised by, a VITA/TCE volunteer.
notes.explanation: By law, tax return preparers must exercise due diligence when preparing or helping to prepare returns.
notes.example: Like a careful driver’s standard of care: not perfection, but what a reasonable volunteer would do.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Due Diligence”, p. 13
notes.evidence: By law, tax return preparers must exercise due diligence in preparing or assisting in the preparation of tax returns. IRS defines due diligence as the degree of care and caution reasonably expected from, and ordinarily exercised by, a volunteer in the VITA/TCE program.

notes.front: What is a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic (LITC)?
notes.back: An independent organisation that helps people whose income is below a certain level resolve tax problems with the Internal Revenue Service.
notes.explanation: Volunteers can refer a taxpayer with unresolved issues to the local clinic, which may be able to help.
notes.example: Like a legal aid clinic, but for tax disputes of people on lower incomes.
notes.source: Publication 4491 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Training Guide, “Low Income Taxpayer Clinic”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: volunteers can provide the taxpayer with a referral to the local Low Income Taxpayer Clinic (LITC) that may be able to help. LITCs are independent from the IRS and the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS). LITCs assist individuals whose income is below a certain level who need to resolve tax problems with the IRS.

notes.front: What is the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS)?
notes.back: An independent organisation within the Internal Revenue Service, led by the National Taxpayer Advocate, that helps taxpayers and protects their rights.
notes.explanation: It offers free help when a tax problem causes financial difficulty, or when the taxpayer has tried and failed to resolve it.
notes.example: Like an ombudsman inside the agency, who steps in when normal channels have failed.
notes.source: Publication 4491 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Training Guide, “The Taxpayer Advocate Service is Here to Help”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) is an independent organization within the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), led by the National Taxpayer Advocate, that helps taxpayers and protect taxpayer rights. TAS offers free help to taxpayers when a tax problem is causing a financial difficulty, when they’ve tried and been unable to resolve their issue with the IRS,

notes.front: How many Volunteer Standards of Conduct are there, and where are they listed?
notes.back: Six, listed on Form 13615.
notes.explanation: The conduct training explains each one and how to report possible violations.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.evidence: An explanation of the six Volunteer Standards of Conduct listed on Form 13615 • Information on how to report possible violations

notes.front: What do SPEC partners certify when they sign the sponsor agreement (Form 13533 or 13533-A)?
notes.back: That they will adhere to the strictest standards of ethical conduct.
notes.explanation: The sponsor also agrees to make sure its volunteers know the standards of conduct and the key principles of privacy and confidentiality.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Form 13533-A, 13533-A FSA Remote Sponsor Agreement, certifying they will adhere to the strictest standards of ethical conduct. By signing this agreement, the sponsor agrees to make certain their volunteers are aware of the standards of conduct and the key principles of privacy and confidentiality.

notes.front: How does an unethical act differ from a lack of knowledge or a simple mistake?
notes.back: An unethical act is done knowingly; an error made without knowing is not unethical.
notes.explanation: A quality reviewer who did not knowingly let an incorrect return be e-filed did not violate the standard.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #4”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Since the quality reviewer did not knowingly allow this return to be e-filed incorrectly, the quality reviewer did not violate this standard. Do not to confuse an unethical action with a lack of knowledge or a simple mistake.

notes.front: A new preparer uses last year’s income limit for a credit, not knowing it has changed, so the credit is claimed wrongly. Has he acted unethically?
notes.back: B: no; a lack of understanding is not unethical.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: any wrong credit breaches VSC #4
B) No: not understanding the law is not an unethical act
C) Yes, but only if the return was accepted
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: VSC #4 is about knowingly preparing false returns. C is wrong: acceptance has nothing to do with intent.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 warns against confusing a lack of knowledge with an unethical action.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Unethical Defined”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Do not confuse an unethical action with a lack of knowledge or a simple mistake.

notes.front: A preparer knows her neighbour’s nephew does not live with him, but lists the nephew as a qualifying child to raise the refund. What is this?
notes.back: B: an unethical act violating the VSC.
notes.choices:
A) A simple mistake
B) An unethical act that violates the VSC
C) Acceptable if the neighbour signs the return
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: she knew the facts. C is wrong: the taxpayer’s signature does not make a knowingly false claim acceptable.
notes.explanation: Knowingly allowing a credit the taxpayer does not qualify for is what makes the act unethical.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Unethical Defined”, p. 2
notes.evidence: However, if Mary knowingly allowed a credit for which the taxpayer did not qualify, Mary committed an unethical act and violated the Volunteer Standards of Conduct.

notes.front: What does VSC #1 require?
notes.back: Follow all Quality Site Requirements.
notes.explanation: The requirements exist to ensure quality, accurate return preparation and consistent operation of sites.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #1”, p. 3
notes.evidence: VSC #1 – Follow all Quality Site Requirements (QSR). The purpose of the Quality Site Requirements (QSR) is to ensure the quality and accuracy of tax return preparation and consistent operation of sites.

notes.front: What does VSC #2 forbid?
notes.back: Accepting payment, asking for donations, or accepting refund payments for federal or state return preparation from customers.
notes.explanation: “Free” means no payment is accepted for the service from the clients served.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: VSC #2 – Do not accept payment, ask for donations, or accept refund payments for federal or state tax return preparation from customers. “Free” means we do not accept payment for our services from the clients we serve.

notes.front: What does VSC #3 forbid?
notes.back: Soliciting business from taxpayers you help, or using their information for any direct or indirect personal benefit to anyone.
notes.explanation: Volunteers must properly use and safeguard taxpayers’ personal information.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: VSC #3 – Do not solicit business from taxpayers you help or use the information gained about them (taxpayer information) for any direct or indirect personal benefit for yourself, any other specific individual or organization. Volunteers must properly use and safeguard taxpayers’ personal information.

notes.front: What does VSC #4 forbid?
notes.back: Knowingly preparing false returns.
notes.explanation: Volunteers must apply tax law correctly to the taxpayer’s situation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #4”, p. 10
notes.evidence: VSC #4 – Do not knowingly prepare false returns. It is imperative that volunteers correctly apply tax law to the taxpayer’s situation.

notes.front: What does VSC #5 forbid?
notes.back: Criminal, infamous, dishonest or notoriously disgraceful conduct, or any other conduct with a negative effect on the programmes.
notes.explanation: SPEC can bar volunteers who engage in such conduct from the programme.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #5”, p. 11
notes.evidence: VSC #5 – Do not engage in criminal, infamous, dishonest, notoriously disgraceful conduct, or any other conduct considered to have a negative effect on the VITA/TCE program. SPEC can prohibit volunteers from participating in the VITA/TCE program if they engage in criminal, infamous, dishonest, or notoriously disgraceful conduct, or any other conduct prejudicial to the government.

notes.front: What does VSC #6 require?
notes.back: Treating all taxpayers in a professional, courteous and respectful manner.
notes.explanation: To safeguard public trust, employees, partners and volunteers must keep the confidence and respect of the people they serve.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #6”, p. 12
notes.evidence: VSC #6 – Treat all taxpayers in a professional, courteous, and respectful manner. To safeguard public trust, Internal Revenue Service employees, partners, and volunteers must maintain the confidence and respect of the people we serve.

notes.front: A volunteer who sells insurance offers a policy to a taxpayer after learning in the interview that she has none. Which standard is breached?
notes.back: B: VSC #3, soliciting business and using taxpayer information for personal benefit.
notes.choices:
A) VSC #2
B) VSC #3
C) VSC #6
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: VSC #2 concerns payment and donations for return preparation. C is wrong: VSC #6 concerns courteous treatment.
notes.explanation: VSC #3 bars using information gained about taxpayers for any direct or indirect personal benefit.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: VSC #3 – Do not solicit business from taxpayers you help or use the information gained about them (taxpayer information) for any direct or indirect personal benefit for yourself, any other specific individual or organization.

notes.front: A preparer accepts $40 “for your trouble” from a taxpayer after finishing her return. Which standard is breached?
notes.back: A: VSC #2, accepting payment for return preparation.
notes.choices:
A) VSC #2
B) VSC #4
C) VSC #5
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: nothing false was prepared. C is wrong: VSC #5 covers criminal or disgraceful conduct generally; payment is VSC #2’s subject.
notes.explanation: VSC #2 bars accepting payment for federal or state return preparation from customers.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: VSC #2 – Do not accept payment, ask for donations, or accept refund payments for federal or state tax return preparation from customers.

notes.front: When does not following a Quality Site Requirement become a violation of the VSC?
notes.back: Only when the volunteer refuses to follow it. If the problem is corrected, it is not a violation.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 explains each Quality Site Requirement in full.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #1”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Non-adherence to any QSR only becomes a violation of the VSC if volunteers refuse to follow the QSR. If the problem is corrected, it is not a violation of the VSC. Refer to Publication 5166, VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, for a full explanation of each QSR.

notes.front: A preparer forgets to use Form 13614-C. The coordinator points it out and he completes one with the taxpayer before going on. Has he violated VSC #1?
notes.back: B: no; the problem was corrected.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: any lapse from a Quality Site Requirement is a violation
B) No: he corrected it; only refusing to follow a requirement is a violation
C) Yes, unless the return was not yet filed
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: non-adherence becomes a violation only on refusal. C is wrong: the test is refusal, not filing status.
notes.explanation: Had he refused to use the form, the lapse would have become a VSC #1 violation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #1”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Non-adherence to any QSR only becomes a violation of the VSC if volunteers refuse to follow the QSR. If the problem is corrected, it is not a violation of the VSC.

notes.front: May a donation or tip jar be placed anywhere at a VITA/TCE site?
notes.back: Only in an area that does not give the impression the site is collecting funds for return preparation.
notes.explanation: Jars in the return preparation or taxpayer waiting area violate VSC #2.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Donation or tip jars located in the return preparation or taxpayer waiting area are a violation of this standard. Donation or tip jars can be placed in another area at the site as long as that area does not give the impression that the site is collecting the funds for return preparation.

notes.front: A library hosting a VITA site puts its book-fund jar on the table at the entrance, where taxpayers sign in. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B: no; the entry area is one of the places a jar cannot be.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: it is the library’s jar, not the site’s
B) No: donation jars cannot be in the entry, waiting, preparation or quality review areas
C) Yes, if a sign says donations are optional
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: the rule is about where the jar is, and an entry-area jar is barred whatever it collects for.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 lists the entry area with the waiting, tax preparation and quality review areas.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Donation or tip jars cannot be in the entry, waiting, tax preparation, or quality review areas.

notes.front: A client offers to pay for her return. How should the volunteer respond?
notes.back: Refuse with a smile: “Thank you, but we cannot accept payment for our services.”
notes.explanation: If someone insists, Publication 4961 suggests recommending cookies or doughnuts for the site.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: A client may offer payment, but always refuse with a smile and say something like, “Thank you, but we cannot accept payment for our services.” If someone insists, recommend cookies or donuts for the site.

notes.front: After a long appointment, a taxpayer leaves a $25 coffee-shop gift card on the preparer’s desk as thanks. What should the preparer do?
notes.back: B: give it back and explain that volunteers cannot accept payment.
notes.choices:
A) Keep it: a gift card is not cash
B) Give it back and explain volunteers cannot accept payment
C) Put it in the site’s donation jar
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: VSC #2 covers payment of any form for the service. C is wrong: the site may not collect payment for preparation either.
notes.explanation: “Free” means no payment is accepted from the clients served.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: “Free” means we do not accept payment for our services from the clients we serve. We do not want to confuse the taxpayer by asking for donations.

notes.front: Why is fee-based return preparation at the VITA site location, while the site is open, a problem?
notes.back: It confuses taxpayers, because VITA is advertised as a free service.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 likens it to tip jars within the preparation space.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Having fee-based preparation at the VITA site location while the VITA site is open is like tip jars within the preparation space. This causes confusion to the taxpayer as VITA is advertised as a free service.

notes.front: Into which bank accounts may a VITA/TCE site request direct deposit of a taxpayer’s refund?
notes.back: Only accounts bearing the taxpayer’s name.
notes.explanation: Refunds must never go into the accounts of volunteers, partners or associated organisations.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Taxpayers’ federal or state refunds must not be deposited into VITA/TCE volunteers', partners' or any associated organizations' personal or business bank/debit card accounts. VITA/TCE sites must only request direct deposit of a taxpayer’s refund into accounts bearing the taxpayer’s name.

notes.front: A taxpayer has no bank account. A kind volunteer offers to receive the refund in her own account and hand over the cash. What is the ruling?
notes.back: B: not allowed; only accounts bearing the taxpayer’s name.
notes.choices:
A) Allowed, as a favour to the taxpayer
B) Not allowed: refunds may go only into accounts in the taxpayer’s name
C) Allowed if the coordinator approves
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: a volunteer’s personal account is expressly barred, whoever approves.
notes.explanation: The rule sits under VSC #2 with the ban on accepting refund payments.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Taxpayers’ federal or state refunds must not be deposited into VITA/TCE volunteers', partners' or any associated organizations' personal or business bank/debit card accounts.

notes.front: A sponsoring organisation’s paid staff prepare VITA returns as part of their jobs. Does that breach VSC #2?
notes.back: No. It is not receiving payment from the customer.
notes.explanation: VSC #2 is about payment from the customers served.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #2”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Some VITA/TCE sites use employees of the sponsoring organization to prepare tax returns as a part of their work duties. This is not considered receiving payment from the customer and is not a violation to this VSC.

notes.front: May volunteers use confidential or nonpublic taxpayer information to engage in financial transactions?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Nor may they allow improper use of taxpayer information to further their own or anyone else’s private interests.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Volunteers may not use confidential or nonpublic information to engage in financial transactions. They cannot allow improper use of taxpayer information to further their own, another persons' or organizations' private interests.

notes.front: A volunteer who is a financial planner slips his business card into each client’s folder of return papers. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B: no; it solicits business from the taxpayers he helps.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: he offers no advice at the site
B) No: it solicits business from taxpayers he helps
C) Yes, if the cards are also on the public notice board
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: soliciting is barred whether or not advice is given. C is wrong: the folder goes to the very taxpayers he helps.
notes.explanation: VSC #3 bars soliciting business from taxpayers the volunteer helps.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: VSC #3 – Do not solicit business from taxpayers you help or use the information gained about them (taxpayer information) for any direct or indirect personal benefit for yourself, any other specific individual or organization.

notes.front: A partner runs a paid bookkeeping business in the same building. Volunteers send every client with self-employment records to it. Which is right?
notes.back: B: a VSC #3 violation.
notes.choices:
A) Fine: it saves clients a trip
B) A VSC #3 violation: taxpayer information from intake is used to benefit the partner
C) Fine, if the partner charges VITA clients less
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: steering clients to the partner’s paid service uses what was learned about them for the organisation’s benefit.
notes.explanation: VSC #3 covers benefit to “any other specific individual or organization”, not only the volunteer.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Do not solicit business from taxpayers you help or use the information gained about them (taxpayer information) for any direct or indirect personal benefit for yourself, any other specific individual or organization.

notes.front: Does SPEC encourage VITA/TCE partnerships with banks or credit unions?
notes.back: Yes, to help unbanked taxpayers open accounts; but sites may not offer RALs or RACs when preparing returns.
notes.explanation: The ban applies when federal or state returns are being prepared.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: SPEC encourages partnering with banks or credit unions to promote unbanked taxpayers to open bank accounts. However, sites and volunteers cannot offer clients refund anticipation loans (RAL) or refund anticipation checks (RAC) when preparing federal or state tax returns.

notes.front: A credit union staffs a table in the same hall as a VITA site, well away from preparation. The credit union offers RACs as part of its business. Is this a VSC #3 violation?
notes.back: B: no; SPEC determined it is not a violation.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: any lender offering RACs must leave the building
B) No: SPEC determined this is not a violation, as long as it is separate from preparation
C) Yes, unless the site stops e-filing
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: SPEC ruled the opposite. C is wrong: e-filing has nothing to do with it. The site itself still may not offer RALs or RACs.
notes.explanation: The separation from the preparation space is what SPEC’s determination turns on.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: SPEC determined having a representative of a bank or credit union present at the same location as a VITA/TCE site but separate from the tax return preparation space is not a violation of VSC #3 even if that bank provides RACs/RALs as part of its overall business.

notes.front: While preparing a return, a volunteer tells the taxpayer she can sign up for a refund anticipation check from the site today. What is wrong?
notes.back: B: sites and volunteers cannot offer RACs when preparing returns.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if the product is free
B) Sites and volunteers cannot offer RACs when preparing returns
C) Only that she should have offered a RAL instead
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the ban does not depend on cost. C is wrong: RALs are banned in the same way.
notes.explanation: The ban names both products and applies to federal and state returns.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: However, sites and volunteers cannot offer clients refund anticipation loans (RAL) or refund anticipation checks (RAC) when preparing federal or state tax returns.

notes.front: Where must a partner bank’s or credit union’s information and enrolment tables be?
notes.back: In a separate space from tax return preparation.
notes.explanation: Their offerings must also be announced in general terms, separately from preparation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Bank or credit union information/enrollment tables must remain in a separate space from tax return preparation. • Bank or credit union offerings must be announced using general terms to potential customers separate from tax return preparation.

notes.front: May a volunteer promote a partner bank to a taxpayer because the return shows she has no bank account and a large refund?
notes.back: No. Volunteers must not promote bank services using information provided to prepare the return.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 gives having no bank account and the refund amount as examples of such information.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #3”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Volunteers must not promote bank or credit union services by using information provided by the taxpayer to prepare a tax return (such as the taxpayer not having a bank account or the amount of the tax refund).

notes.front: Under section 7216 of the Internal Revenue Code, when must a volunteer site secure the taxpayer’s consent?
notes.back: When it uses or discloses taxpayer data for purposes other than current, prior or subsequent year return preparation.
notes.explanation: There are several types of consent, including the Global Carry Forward Consent.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Securing consent”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Under Internal Revenue Code § 7216, all volunteer sites using or disclosing taxpayer data for purposes other than current, prior, or subsequent year tax return preparation must secure a consent from the taxpayer. There are several types of consents: Global Carry Forward Consent, Relational EFIN Consent, and Use and Disclosure Consents.

notes.front: A site wants to pass its clients’ names and addresses to a partner food bank for outreach. What does it need first?
notes.back: B: each taxpayer’s consent.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the food bank is a charity
B) Each taxpayer’s consent, because the use is not return preparation
C) Only the coordinator’s approval
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: any use or disclosure beyond return preparation needs the taxpayer’s consent, whoever receives it.
notes.explanation: Section 7216 requires consent for purposes other than current, prior or subsequent year preparation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Securing consent”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Under Internal Revenue Code § 7216, all volunteer sites using or disclosing taxpayer data for purposes other than current, prior, or subsequent year tax return preparation must secure a consent from the taxpayer.

notes.front: May a site publish the total number of returns it prepared, for fundraising or publicity, without taxpayers’ consent?
notes.back: Yes, if it includes no personally identifiable information and no data from fewer than ten returns.
notes.explanation: This is an exception to the consent rule for aggregate data.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Exceptions to required consents”, p. 10
notes.evidence: (aggregate data) for fundraising, marketing, and publicity are not required to secure taxpayers’ consent. This information cannot include any Personally Identifiable Information (PII), such as the taxpayer’s name, SSN/ITIN, address or other personal information, and does not disclose information containing data from fewer than ten tax returns.

notes.front: A site’s flyer says “We got our clients $3.2 million in refunds last year”. Does the aggregate-data exception cover it?
notes.back: B: no; statistics reflecting dollar amounts of refunds are outside the exception.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: no client is named
B) No: the exception does not cover marketing that shows dollar amounts of refunds
C) Yes, if more than ten returns are included
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: leaving out names and using ten or more returns are necessary, but dollar amounts in marketing still fall outside.
notes.explanation: The exception is for the total number of returns, not their dollar amounts.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Exceptions to required consents”, p. 10
notes.evidence: This exception does not apply to the use or disclosure in marketing or advertising of statistical compilations containing or reflecting dollar amounts of refunds, credits, rebates, or related percentages.

notes.front: What is the maximum penalty for violating section 7216 of the Internal Revenue Code?
notes.back: A misdemeanour: up to one year in prison, a fine of up to $1,000, or both, plus prosecution costs.
notes.explanation: Section 7216(a) imposes criminal penalties on preparers who knowingly or recklessly make unauthorised disclosures or uses.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Exceptions to required consents”, p. 10
notes.evidence: tax return preparers who knowingly or recklessly make unauthorized disclosures or uses of information furnished in connection with the preparation of an income tax return. A violation of IRC 7216 is a misdemeanor, with a maximum penalty of up to one year imprisonment or a fine of not more than $1,000, or both, together with the cost of prosecution.

notes.front: A volunteer recklessly posts a photo of a client’s return, showing her income, on social media. What legal exposure does section 7216 create?
notes.back: B: a misdemeanour, with up to one year in prison, a fine up to $1,000, or both.
notes.choices:
A) None: volunteers are not paid preparers
B) A misdemeanour: up to one year in prison, a fine up to $1,000, or both
C) A civil fine only, with no criminal penalty
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: section 7216(a) covers tax return preparers who disclose knowingly or recklessly. C is wrong: the penalties are criminal.
notes.explanation: Reckless, not only knowing, disclosure is covered.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “IRC 7216(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: IRC 7216(a) - Imposes criminal penalties on tax return preparers who knowingly or recklessly make unauthorized disclosures or uses of information furnished in connection with the preparation of an income tax return. A violation of IRC 7216(a) is a misdemeanor, with a maximum penalty of up to one year imprisonment or a fine of not more than $1,000, or both,

notes.front: Why does Publication 4961 warn volunteers against bending the law to help taxpayers?
notes.back: It will cause problems down the road for the taxpayers.
notes.explanation: Trust in the Internal Revenue Service and the sponsoring organisation is put at risk when ethical standards are not followed.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #4”, p. 10
notes.evidence: While it can be a temptation for a volunteer to bend the law to help taxpayers, this will cause problems down the road for the taxpayers. Volunteers must not knowingly prepare false returns. Trust in the IRS and the local sponsoring organization is jeopardized when ethical standards are not followed.

notes.front: A volunteer’s fraud leaves a taxpayer with extra tax. If the taxpayer seeks damages from the SPEC partner, who does the Internal Revenue Service pursue for the tax, interest and penalties?
notes.back: Still the taxpayer.
notes.explanation: The taxpayer may seek damages from the partner under state or local law, but that does not change who owes the tax.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #4”, p. 10
notes.evidence: In addition, the taxpayer may seek damages under state or local law from the SPEC partner for the volunteer’s fraudulent actions. Even so, the IRS would still seek payment of the additional taxes, interest, and penalties from the taxpayer.

notes.front: A volunteer knowingly added a false deduction. Two years later the taxpayer receives a bill for tax, interest and penalties. Which is true?
notes.back: B: the taxpayer must still pay, and may seek money from the partner.
notes.choices:
A) The volunteer’s fraud cancels the bill
B) The taxpayer must still pay, though she may seek money from the SPEC partner
C) The SPEC partner pays the bill directly
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the fraud does not remove the tax. C is wrong: the bill stays with the taxpayer; any claim against the partner is hers to bring.
notes.explanation: Fraudulent returns can mean years of dealing with the agency while paying the extra tax plus interest and penalties.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “Taxpayer Impact”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Fraudulent returns that report incorrect income, credits, or deductions can result in many years of interaction with the IRS as the taxpayer tries to pay the additional tax plus interest and penalties. This can result in an extreme burden for the taxpayer.

notes.front: A preparer deliberately leaves off a client’s side-job income. The quality reviewer does not notice, and the return is filed. Who violated VSC #4?
notes.back: B: only the preparer, who acted knowingly.
notes.choices:
A) Both of them
B) Only the preparer
C) Only the quality reviewer, who should have caught it
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: a reviewer who did not knowingly let an incorrect return through has not violated VSC #4.
notes.explanation: VSC #4 turns on knowingly preparing a false return.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #4”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Since the quality reviewer did not knowingly allow this return to be e-filed incorrectly, the quality reviewer did not violate this standard.

notes.front: Any suspicion of identity theft occurring at a VITA/TCE site must be reported to which two bodies?
notes.back: Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration.
notes.explanation: The agency treats this as a very serious crime and has measures to detect it at sites.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Identity Theft”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Any suspicion of identity theft occurring at a VITA/TCE site must be reported to IRS Criminal Investigation (CI) and Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA). The IRS considers this a very serious crime and put measures in place to detect possible identity theft situations at VITA/TCE sites.
uses: Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration

notes.front: A volunteer sees a colleague photographing clients’ Social Security cards with his phone. She suspects identity theft. Where must the suspicion be reported?
notes.back: B: to Criminal Investigation and TIGTA.
notes.choices:
A) Only to the colleague, to give him a chance to explain
B) To Criminal Investigation and TIGTA
C) Nowhere, unless a refund is actually stolen
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the rule requires a report, not a private word. C is wrong: any suspicion must be reported, not only proven theft.
notes.explanation: The rule covers “any suspicion” of identity theft at a site.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Identity Theft”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Any suspicion of identity theft occurring at a VITA/TCE site must be reported to IRS Criminal Investigation (CI) and Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA).
uses: Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration

notes.front: In an email reporting a suspected violation to SPEC headquarters, which three details about yourself should you give?
notes.back: Your name, your contact number and your site name.
notes.explanation: The email also needs a detailed description of the incident.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #4”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The email should include your name, contact number, site name, and a detailed ts.voltax@irs.gov description of the incident

notes.front: In the detailed description of an incident reported to SPEC headquarters, which three facts should be included?
notes.back: The individual’s full name, the date of the incident, and the number of taxpayers affected.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 adds “if applicable” to the number of taxpayers affected.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “External Referral Process”, p. 15
notes.evidence: a detailed description of the incident including the individual's full name, date the incident occurred and the number of taxpayers affected by the violation if applicable.

notes.front: You learn that another volunteer has engaged in criminal conduct. What must you do?
notes.back: Report it immediately to your coordinator and email SPEC headquarters, copying the partner and local territory office as appropriate.
notes.explanation: The same applies to any violation of the Volunteer Standards of Conduct.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #5”, p. 12
notes.evidence: If you have information indicating that another volunteer has engaged in criminal conduct or violated any of the Volunteer Standards of Conduct, immediately report such information to your coordinator and email SPEC headquarters at ts.voltax@irs.gov and copy the partner and the local SPEC territory office as appropriate.

notes.front: What happens to volunteers who perform egregious activities?
notes.back: They are barred from volunteering for VITA/TCE and may be added to a registry of barred volunteers.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 sets this out as the consequence under VSC #5.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Consequences”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Volunteers performing egregious activities are barred from volunteering for the VITA/TCE program and may be added to a registry of barred volunteers.

notes.front: A volunteer greeter is convicted of shoplifting, and a local radio report names the VITA site where she helps. Can this affect her VITA/TCE role?
notes.back: B: yes; VSC #5 covers criminal conduct with a negative effect on the programme.
notes.choices:
A) No: the conduct had nothing to do with tax preparation
B) Yes: criminal conduct with a negative effect on the programme falls under VSC #5
C) Only if a taxpayer complains
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: VSC #5 is not limited to conduct at the site. C is wrong: no complaint is needed.
notes.explanation: Volunteers must avoid interactions that discredit the programme.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #5”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Volunteers must take care to avoid interactions that discredit the program. A taxpayer may look to state or local law to seek money from the SPEC partner for a volunteer’s fraudulent actions.

notes.front: Who is an “unauthorized alien” for VITA/TCE volunteering purposes?
notes.back: A person not lawfully admitted to the United States for either permanent residence or employment.
notes.explanation: Allowing an unauthorised alien to volunteer at a site is prohibited.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Consequences”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Allowing an unauthorized alien to volunteer at a VITA/TCE site is prohibited. An “unauthorized alien” is defined as a person not lawfully admitted into the United States for either permanent residence or employment.

notes.front: Must coordinators validate volunteers’ legal status in the United States?
notes.back: No. They check identity with photo identification; volunteers certify legal residence by signing Form 13615.
notes.explanation: Checking identity is required of coordinators; validating legal status is not.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Consequences”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Coordinators are required to ask for proof of identity with a government-issued photo ID for each volunteer. However, coordinators or partners are not required to validate the legal status of volunteers. Therefore, by signing Form 13615, volunteers are certifying that they are legal residents of the United States.

notes.front: Taxpayers have waited a long time and volunteers are stretched. What does VSC #6 ask of volunteers?
notes.back: To remain calm and create a peaceful, friendly atmosphere.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 notes that stress on both sides can make patience run short.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #6”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Volunteers may also experience stress due to the volume of taxpayers needing service. This situation can make patience run short. It is important to remain calm and create a peaceful and friendly atmosphere.

notes.front: A taxpayer sees that this year’s refund is half of last year’s and, in front of the queue, loudly accuses the volunteer of losing him money. What should the volunteer do?
notes.back: B: stay calm, explain courteously, and involve the coordinator if needed.
notes.choices:
A) Tell him to find another site
B) Stay calm, courteously explain that every return is different, and involve the coordinator if needed
C) Add a deduction to raise the refund
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: it is not professional or courteous. C is wrong: knowingly adding a false deduction breaches VSC #4.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 suggests taking a deep breath before explaining.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #6”, p. 12
notes.evidence: In this situation, you should take a deep breath and courteously explain that every return is different. If necessary, involve the coordinator.

notes.front: In federally assisted programmes, discrimination against taxpayers is prohibited on the basis of race, color, {{c1::national origin (including Limited English Proficiency)}}, disability, sex (in education programs or activities), age or reprisal.
notes.back: National origin (including Limited English Proficiency).
notes.explanation: It applies to programmes and activities receiving federal financial assistance.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer Civil Rights”, p. 13
notes.evidence: discrimination against taxpayers on the basis of race, color, national origin (including Limited English Proficiency), disability, sex (in education programs or activities), age or reprisal is prohibited in programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance.

notes.front: Discrimination against taxpayers on the basis of race, color, national origin (including Limited English Proficiency), {{c1::disability}}, sex (in education programs or activities), age or reprisal is prohibited in programmes receiving federal financial assistance.
notes.back: Disability.
notes.explanation: Taxpayers with a disability may request a reasonable accommodation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer Civil Rights”, p. 13
notes.evidence: or activities), age or reprisal is prohibited in programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance. Persons with disabilities and/or limited English proficiency should be able to participate in or benefit from programs and services that IRS supports. Taxpayers with a disability may request a reasonable accommodation

notes.front: Among the grounds on which discrimination is prohibited, sex is listed with the limit “{{c1::in education programs or activities}}”.
notes.back: In education programs or activities.
notes.explanation: The other grounds carry no such limit in the list.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer Civil Rights”, p. 13
notes.evidence: national origin (including Limited English Proficiency), disability, sex (in education programs or activities), age or reprisal is prohibited in programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance.

notes.front: The last ground in the list of prohibited discrimination, after race, color, national origin, disability, sex and age, is {{c1::reprisal}}.
notes.back: Reprisal.
notes.explanation: The list applies to programmes and activities receiving federal financial assistance.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer Civil Rights”, p. 13
notes.evidence: national origin (including Limited English Proficiency), disability, sex (in education programs or activities), age or reprisal is prohibited in programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance.

notes.front: What may taxpayers with limited English proficiency request to access VITA/TCE services?
notes.back: Language assistance.
notes.explanation: Taxpayers with a disability may likewise request a reasonable accommodation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer Civil Rights”, p. 13
notes.evidence: Taxpayers with a disability may request a reasonable accommodation and taxpayers with limited English proficiency may request language assistance to access services.

notes.front: A taxpayer who uses a wheelchair asks the site to meet her at a ground-floor table instead of the upstairs room. Who is responsible for seeing that reasonable requests like this are granted at a federally assisted site?
notes.back: A: the coordinator.
notes.choices:
A) The coordinator
B) Nobody: sites need not change their layout
C) The taxpayer, who must find an accessible site
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: coordinators must ensure reasonable accommodation requests from qualified individuals with disabilities are granted.
notes.explanation: Coordinators must also take reasonable steps to give people with limited English meaningful access.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer Civil Rights”, p. 13
notes.evidence: Coordinators at federally assisted sites are responsible for ensuring that reasonable requests for accommodation are granted when the requests are made by qualified individuals with disabilities and that reasonable steps are taken to ensure that LEP persons have meaningful access to its programs or activities.

notes.front: What does “doing your part” under due diligence include?
notes.back: Confirming the taxpayer’s (and joint-filing spouse’s) identity, and helping them understand and meet their tax responsibilities.
notes.explanation: The aim is that the information on the return is correct and complete.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Due Diligence”, p. 13
notes.evidence: This means, as a volunteer, you must do your part when preparing or quality reviewing a tax return to ensure the information on the return is correct and complete. Doing your part includes confirming a taxpayer’s (and/or spouse, if married filing jointly) identity and providing top-quality service by helping them understand and meet their tax responsibilities.

notes.front: May tax law certified volunteers rely on what a taxpayer tells them without documents to verify it?
notes.back: Generally yes, in good faith; but they must ask the taxpayer to clarify anything that seems inconsistent or incomplete.
notes.explanation: Asking for clarification is part of due diligence.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Due Diligence”, p. 13
notes.evidence: Generally, IRS tax law certified volunteers may rely in good faith on information from a taxpayer without requiring documentation as verification. However, part of due diligence requires volunteers to ask a taxpayer to clarify information that may appear to be inconsistent or incomplete.

notes.front: When reviewing information for accuracy, what should volunteers ask themselves?
notes.back: Whether the information is unusual or questionable.
notes.explanation: This check sits beside the general permission to rely on taxpayers in good faith.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Due Diligence”, p. 13
notes.evidence: When reviewing information for its accuracy, volunteers need to ask themselves if the information is unusual or questionable.

notes.front: A taxpayer says her daughter lived with her all year, but her intake sheet gives the daughter a different address. What should the volunteer do?
notes.back: B: ask the taxpayer to clarify.
notes.choices:
A) Rely on what the taxpayer said, since documents are not required
B) Ask the taxpayer to clarify the inconsistency
C) Refuse service at once
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: good-faith reliance does not cover information that appears inconsistent. C is wrong: the first step is to clarify, not to refuse.
notes.explanation: Due diligence requires asking about information that appears inconsistent or incomplete.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Due Diligence”, p. 13
notes.evidence: However, part of due diligence requires volunteers to ask a taxpayer to clarify information that may appear to be inconsistent or incomplete.

notes.front: What should a volunteer do if at any time they become uncomfortable with the information a taxpayer provides?
notes.back: Not prepare the return, and tell the site coordinator the reason.
notes.explanation: Publication 5838 puts this under due diligence, straight after asking whether the information is unusual or questionable.
notes.source: Publication 5838 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Intake/Interview and Quality Review Handbook, “1-3: Due Diligence”, p. 5
notes.evidence: If at any time you become uncomfortable with the information provided by the taxpayer, you should not prepare the tax return and inform the site coordinator of the reason for not preparing the tax return.

notes.front: A taxpayer’s account of his business income keeps changing, and the volunteer senses he is not telling the truth. What should she do?
notes.back: B: a thorough interview, then the coordinator; she is not obliged to prepare it.
notes.choices:
A) Ignore it: volunteers rely on taxpayers in good faith
B) Interview him thoroughly, refer him to the coordinator if that does not resolve it, and know she need not prepare the return
C) Prepare the return but add a note to the file
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a volunteer who senses untruth should not ignore it. C is wrong: an uncomfortable volunteer is not obliged to prepare the return.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 sets out these steps for a taxpayer who may not be telling the truth.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “What if the taxpayer is not telling the truth?”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Conduct a thorough interview to ensure there is no misunderstanding. If that does not resolve the matter, refer the taxpayer to the coordinator. Remember, if a volunteer is not comfortable with the information provided from the taxpayer, the volunteer is not obligated to prepare the return.

notes.front: When in doubt, which two people does Publication 4961 say a volunteer can ask for help?
notes.back: The coordinator and a tax preparer with more experience.
notes.explanation: Another option is to reschedule, or suggest the taxpayer return when a more experienced preparer is available.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Due Diligence”, p. 13
notes.evidence: When in doubt, make an effort to find the answer • Seek assistance from the coordinator • Seek assistance from a tax preparer with more experience • Reschedule or suggest the taxpayer come back when a more experienced tax preparer is available

notes.front: Among the when-in-doubt resources, the VITA/TCE Hotline number is 1-800-829-VITA ({{c1::8482}}).
notes.explanation: The same list includes researching the agency’s website.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Due Diligence”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Research www.irs.gov • Call the VITA/TCE Hotline at 1-800-829-VITA (8482)

notes.front: Who operates the VITA/TCE programme, and what is the Internal Revenue Service’s role?
notes.back: Sponsoring partners and coalitions outside the agency operate it; the Internal Revenue Service provides oversight.
notes.explanation: The oversight is there to protect the programmes’ integrity and maintain taxpayer confidence.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Who enforces the standards?”, p. 14
notes.evidence: The VITA/TCE program is operated by sponsoring partners and/or coalitions outside the IRS. However, IRS is responsible for providing oversight to protect the VITA/TCE programs’ integrity and to maintain taxpayer confidence.

notes.front: SPEC finds conduct at a site that violates the standards and recommends corrective action. The site will not remedy it. What follows?
notes.back: B: SPEC ends the relationship and removes government property.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more: recommendations are advisory
B) SPEC discontinues its relationship and removes government property from the site
C) The site is fined $1,000
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: refusal to remedy has a stated consequence. C is wrong: no such fine is described.
notes.explanation: In cases of wrongdoing, SPEC may also terminate a VITA/TCE grant.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “How are the standards enforced?”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If conduct violating the standards occurs at a VITA/TCE site, IRS-SPEC will recommend corrective actions. If the site cannot or will not remedy the conduct, then IRS-SPEC will discontinue its relationship and remove any government property from the site. In cases of wrongdoing, illegal conduct, and/or management practices that violate the VSC, IRS-SPEC may terminate a VITA/TCE grant.

notes.front: Which violations by another volunteer must you report?
notes.back: Those that raise substantial questions about the volunteer’s honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a tax preparer.
notes.explanation: Reporting is how volunteers help sustain confidence in the programme.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Volunteer’s role in reporting questionable activity”, p. 14
notes.evidence: To sustain confidence in the VITA/ TCE program, you must report violations that raise substantial questions about another volunteer’s honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a tax preparer.

notes.front: Is the list of consequences for failing to comply with the VSC on Form 13615 complete?
notes.back: No. Failure “could result in, but is not limited to” the listed consequences.
notes.explanation: The list starts with removal from all VITA/TCE programmes.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “Standards of Conduct”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Failure to comply with these standards could result in, but is not limited to, the following: • Removal from all VITA/TCE programs

notes.front: Which listed consequence of breaking the VSC bars future VITA/TCE activity indefinitely?
notes.back: Inclusion in the Volunteer Registry.
notes.explanation: Form 13615 lists it right after removal from all VITA/TCE programmes.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “Standards of Conduct”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Removal from all VITA/TCE programs • Inclusion in the IRS Volunteer Registry to bar future VITA/TCE activity indefinitely

notes.front: Which of the sponsoring partner’s site identifiers can be deactivated as a consequence of breaking the VSC?
notes.back: Its VITA/TCE electronic filing identification number.
notes.explanation: Form 13615 lists this among the consequences that fall on the sponsoring partner’s site.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “Standards of Conduct”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Deactivation of your sponsoring partner’s site VITA/TCE electronic filing identification number (EFIN)

notes.front: Which consequence of breaking the VSC takes things away from the site itself?
notes.back: Removal of all the agency’s products, supplies, loaned equipment and taxpayer information from the site.
notes.explanation: Form 13615 lists it between deactivation of the site’s filing number and termination of the partnership.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “Standards of Conduct”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Removal of all IRS products, supplies, loaned equipment, and taxpayer information from your site

notes.front: Which two listed consequences of breaking the VSC end the sponsoring organisation’s links with the agency?
notes.back: Termination of its partnership, and termination of grant funds to the sponsoring partner.
notes.explanation: Form 13615 lists the two one after the other.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “Standards of Conduct”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Termination of your sponsoring organization’s partnership with the IRS • Termination of grant funds from the IRS to your sponsoring partner

notes.front: For which kinds of investigation can a volunteer’s conduct be referred as a consequence of breaking the VSC?
notes.back: TIGTA and criminal investigations.
notes.explanation: This is the last item in Form 13615’s list of consequences.
notes.source: Form 13615 (Rev. 10-2025), Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs, “Standards of Conduct”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Referral of your conduct for potential TIGTA and criminal investigations

notes.front: What is the purpose of the Volunteer Registry?
notes.back: To notify SPEC employees of volunteers and partners who were removed from the VITA/TCE programme.
notes.explanation: It records partner or individual names, locations, and affiliated agencies or sponsors.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Volunteer Registry”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The purpose of the registry is to notify IRS-SPEC employees of volunteers and partners who were removed from the VITA/TCE program. The registry will include partner or individual names, locations, and affiliated agency or sponsors.

notes.front: For how long are volunteers and partners on the Volunteer Registry unable to take part in VITA/TCE?
notes.back: Indefinitely.
notes.explanation: The registry records names, locations, and affiliated agencies or sponsors.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Volunteer Registry”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The registry will include partner or individual names, locations, and affiliated agency or sponsors. Volunteers and/or partners on this list are unable to participate in VITA/TCE program indefinitely.

notes.front: What are two willful actions Publication 4961 gives as egregious?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: harming taxpayers; refusing to follow Quality Site Requirements; accepting payment; using taxpayer information for gain; knowingly preparing false returns.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 says egregious actions “include, but are not limited to” these willful actions, so the list is open.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Volunteer Registry”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Creating harm to taxpayers, volunteers or IRS employees • Refusing to adhere to all Quality Site Requirements • Accepting payments for return preparation at VITA/TCE sites • Using taxpayer personal information for personal gain • Knowingly preparing false returns

notes.front: A preparer released for knowingly filing false returns is added to the Volunteer Registry. Next season he applies to a different partner in another state. What is the position?
notes.back: B: he cannot take part; those on the registry are barred indefinitely.
notes.choices:
A) He may volunteer: the registry applies only to his old partner
B) He cannot take part in VITA/TCE: the bar is indefinite
C) He may volunteer after passing the conduct test again
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the bar is from the VITA/TCE programme, not one partner. C is wrong: retesting does not lift an indefinite bar.
notes.explanation: The registry exists so SPEC employees know who has been removed.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Volunteer Registry”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The purpose of the registry is to notify IRS-SPEC employees of volunteers and partners who were removed from the VITA/TCE program. The registry will include partner or individual names, locations, and affiliated agency or sponsors. Volunteers and/or partners on this list are unable to participate in VITA/TCE program indefinitely.

notes.front: What has one volunteer’s unethical behaviour led SPEC to do to some tax sites, and with what effect on the community?
notes.back: Close them, leaving taxpayers without access to free tax preparation in their community.
notes.explanation: One volunteer’s conduct can cast suspicion on the whole programme.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “What is the impact on VITA/TCE programs?”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Unfortunately, one volunteer’s unethical behavior can cast a cloud of suspicion on the VITA/TCE program as a whole. IRS-SPEC has closed tax sites due to unethical behavior, which left taxpayers without access to free tax preparation in their community.

notes.front: In general, who is a volunteer’s first point of contact for resolving problems?
notes.back: The coordinator.
notes.explanation: If the volunteer feels an ethical issue cannot be handled by the coordinator, they email SPEC headquarters.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “What if an unethical situation is discovered at a site?”, p. 14
notes.evidence: In general, the coordinator is the first point of contact for resolving any problems that a volunteer may encounter. If a volunteer feels an ethical issue can’t be handled by the coordinator, the volunteer should e-mail SPEC headquarters at ts.voltax@irs.gov

notes.front: A volunteer suspects her own coordinator is taking cash from clients. Where should she take the concern?
notes.back: B: email SPEC headquarters, copying the partner and territory office as appropriate.
notes.choices:
A) Only to the coordinator, as first point of contact
B) By email to SPEC headquarters, copying the partner and the local SPEC territory office as appropriate
C) Nowhere until she has proof
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: an issue the coordinator cannot handle goes to headquarters. C is wrong: suspicious behaviour should be reported immediately.
notes.explanation: The coordinator is the usual first contact, but not for an issue the coordinator cannot handle.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “What if an unethical situation is discovered at a site?”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If a volunteer feels an ethical issue can’t be handled by the coordinator, the volunteer should e-mail SPEC headquarters at ts.voltax@irs.gov and copy the partner and the local SPEC territory office as appropriate.

notes.front: When must volunteers, coordinators or taxpayers use VolTax?
notes.back: When they identify potential problems at the partner, site or volunteer level that may require independent scrutiny.
notes.explanation: The report goes by email to SPEC headquarters, with the partner and local territory office copied as appropriate.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “What if an unethical situation is discovered at a site?”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If volunteers, coordinators, or taxpayers identify potential problems at the partner, site, or volunteer level that may require independent scrutiny, they must report these issues using the external referral process (VolTax) by emailing SPEC headquarters at ts.voltax@irs.gov. Copy the partner and the local SPEC territory office as appropriate.

notes.front: A coordinator determines a volunteer has violated the VSC. What must the coordinator do?
notes.back: Immediately remove the volunteer from all site activities, deactivate their software access, and notify the partner and SPEC.
notes.explanation: Both the partner and SPEC must receive the details of the violation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Coordinator’s Responsibility”, p. 15
notes.evidence: If a coordinator determines a volunteer has violated the Volunteer Standards of Conduct, the coordinator needs to immediately remove the volunteer from all site activities and deactivate their access to tax preparation software. In addition, notify both the partner and IRS-SPEC with the details of the violation.

notes.front: By which two routes can a coordinator notify SPEC of a violation?
notes.back: By contacting the local SPEC territory office, or by using VolTax.
notes.explanation: A territory that is contacted uses the internal referral process to raise the matter to headquarters.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Coordinator’s Responsibility”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The coordinator can notify IRS-SPEC by either contacting their local SPEC territory office or using the external referral process (VolTax). If the coordinator contacts the territory, the territory will use the internal referral process to elevate the referral to headquarters.

notes.front: A coordinator confirms that a preparer has been depositing clients’ refunds into his own account. What comes first?
notes.back: B: remove him at once, deactivate his access, and notify the partner and SPEC.
notes.choices:
A) Let him finish the season, then report
B) Remove him from all site activities at once, deactivate his software access, and notify the partner and SPEC
C) Warn him privately and move him to greeting
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: removal must be immediate, and both the partner and SPEC must be told.
notes.explanation: These steps apply whenever a coordinator determines that a volunteer violated the VSC.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Coordinator’s Responsibility”, p. 15
notes.evidence: the coordinator needs to immediately remove the volunteer from all site activities and deactivate their access to tax preparation software. In addition, notify both the partner and IRS-SPEC with the details of the violation.

notes.front: What must every VITA and TCE site display so taxpayers know they can make a referral?
notes.back: Publication 4836, in a visible location (or D-143 at Tax-Aide sites).
notes.explanation: The poster makes taxpayers aware that they can report problems.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “External Referral Process”, p. 15
notes.evidence: All VITA and TCE sites are required to display Publication 4836 (en-sp), or D-143 for AARP sites, in a visible location to ensure taxpayer awareness of the ability to make a referral.

notes.front: What does it mean when an e-filed return is accepted?
notes.back: Only that the required fields are complete and no duplicate return exists; it may not be accurate.
notes.explanation: An incorrect return can still cause the taxpayer financial stress.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “What is the impact on taxpayers?”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Although a return is accepted, it may not be accurate. Acceptance merely means the required fields are complete and that no duplicate returns exist. However, an incorrect return can cause a taxpayer financial stress.

notes.front: A volunteer says: “The return was accepted, so the credit we claimed must have been right.” Is that sound?
notes.back: B: no; acceptance does not confirm accuracy.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: acceptance confirms accuracy
B) No: acceptance means only that required fields are complete and there is no duplicate
C) Yes, once the refund arrives
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: an accepted return, even one that has been paid, may still be inaccurate.
notes.explanation: A taxpayer is responsible for paying only the correct amount of tax due under the law.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “What is the impact on taxpayers?”, p. 16
notes.evidence: A taxpayer is responsible for paying only the correct amount of tax due under the law. Although a return is accepted, it may not be accurate. Acceptance merely means the required fields are complete and that no duplicate returns exist.

notes.front: For relief from tax collection, what does “significant hardship” mean?
notes.back: Serious deprivation, not simply economic or personal inconvenience.
notes.explanation: Even if collection stops, interest and penalties keep accruing until the balance is paid in full.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “How might the taxpayer find relief?”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Significant hardship means serious deprivation, not simply economic or personal inconvenience to the taxpayer. Although, collection action may stop, interest and penalties will continue to accrue until the balance is paid in full.

notes.front: How does a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic differ from the Taxpayer Advocate Service in whom it helps?
notes.back: LITCs represent taxpayers below an income level with tax problems; TAS helps when a problem causes financial hardship or is systemic.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 lists both as referrals for taxpayers seeking relief.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “How might the taxpayer find relief?”, p. 16
notes.evidence: LITCs are organizations that represent and advocate for taxpayers who have tax problems with the IRS, who's incomes are below a certain level. TAS can help you if your tax problem is causing a financial hardship or a systemic issue.

notes.front: A taxpayer has tried for months without success to fix an account problem with the agency, and it is now causing her significant hardship. Where does Publication 4961’s referral chart send her?
notes.back: A: the Taxpayer Advocate Service.

A) The Taxpayer Advocate Service
B) Form 3949-A
C) The VITA/TCE Hotline

notes.explanation: The chart says TAS can offer special help to a taxpayer experiencing significant hardship because of a tax problem.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Resolving Problems”, p. 19

notes.front: What must volunteers remind taxpayers of when they sign Form 1040 or Form 8879?
notes.back: That they are stating under penalty of perjury that the return is accurate to the best of their knowledge.
notes.explanation: The reminder applies whether the taxpayer signs Form 1040 itself or the e-file signature authorisation.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer review and acknowledgment”, p. 17
notes.evidence: Volunteers must remind taxpayers that when they sign the return (either by signing Form 1040, U.S. Individual Income Tax Return or signing Form 8879, IRS e-file Signature Authorization), they are stating under penalty of perjury that the return is accurate to the best of their knowledge.

notes.front: A taxpayer signs Form 8879 saying, “It’s your return, not mine; if it’s wrong that’s on you.” How should the volunteer respond?
notes.back: B: remind him of the penalty-of-perjury statement he is making.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: the preparer is responsible for the contents
B) Remind him that by signing he states under penalty of perjury that the return is accurate to the best of his knowledge
C) Sign Form 8879 on his behalf instead
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the taxpayer’s signature carries his own declaration. C is wrong: the taxpayer signs the authorisation.
notes.explanation: The declaration he signs says he examined the return and believes it true, correct and complete.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer review and acknowledgment”, p. 17
notes.evidence: For the Taxpayer: “Under penalties of perjury, I declare that I have examined this return and accompanying schedules and statements, and to the best of my knowledge and belief, they are true, correct, and complete.”

notes.front: On what is the preparer’s declaration on a tax return based?
notes.back: On all information of which the preparer has any knowledge.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two disclosure statements on a return, beside the taxpayer’s.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “Taxpayer review and acknowledgment”, p. 17
notes.evidence: For the Preparer: “Declaration of preparer (other than the taxpayer) is based on all information of which preparer has any knowledge.”
